subject: mathematics
question_text: If A is the matrix with rows (−1, 2) and (0, 1), then find AAᵀ.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), chapter 5 MATRICES, Very Short Answer question 12, book p.33. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1 split gives one mark to writing the transpose and one to the row-by-column product, because writing Aᵀ with the entries in the wrong places is where this question is usually lost. CHECKED TWO WAYS: the four entries were computed position by position (5, 2, 2, 1), and the answer was then tested against two properties it must have — AAᵀ is symmetric, and det(AAᵀ) = (det A)² = (−1)² = 1, which the answer 5(1) − 2(2) = 1 satisfies. Related card in the same unit: ts_ipe_m1a_mat_vsaq_a_plus_transpose asks for A + A′ and AA′ for a different 2×2 matrix, so the two are not duplicates. Paper position: Maths-1A Section A runs Q1 to Q10 at 2 marks each, all compulsory, under the 2026-27 pattern. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would find AAᵀ for this 2×2 matrix.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Write Aᵀ
steps.margin_note: First mark. Aᵀ exchanges rows with columns: the entry in row 1 column 2 moves to row 2 column 1. Write it out before multiplying anything.
steps.memory_tip: Row 1 of A becomes column 1 of Aᵀ. The two diagonal entries never move.
lines: A is 2×2, so AAᵀ is 2×2 as well.

recall.must_convey: That Aᵀ is written by exchanging rows with columns, giving rows (−1, 0) and (2, 1).
accept: write the transpose by making rows into columns
A transpose has rows minus one zero and two one
the two off diagonal entries swap places
rows ni columns ga marchi A transpose rasukovali
transpose first, the diagonal stays the same

steps.why: The transpose is defined position by position: the entry aᵢⱼ of A becomes the entry in row j column i of Aᵀ. Writing it out is what stops the two indices being swapped by accident.
common_mistakes: Reversing the order of the rows instead of exchanging rows with columns.
Changing the signs of the entries while transposing.

steps.label: Multiply A by Aᵀ
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Each entry is a row of A times a column of Aᵀ. The answer must come out symmetric — AAᵀ always does — which is a free check.
steps.memory_tip: AAᵀ is always symmetric. If the two off-diagonal entries differ, one of them is wrong.

recall.must_convey: That the product is taken row by column, giving the symmetric matrix with rows (5, 2) and (2, 1).
accept: multiply row by column to get five two and two one
the answer is five, two, two, one and it is symmetric
first row times first column gives one plus four which is five
row into column multiply cheste five two two one vasthundi
AA transpose is the symmetric matrix with five on the top left

steps.why: Matrix multiplication pairs a row of the first matrix with a column of the second. Because the second matrix is Aᵀ, each entry is a dot product of two rows of A, which is why the result is symmetric.
common_mistakes: Multiplying the matrices entry by entry instead of row by column.
Computing AᵀA, which is a different matrix here.
